name: 02_en_history

context.subject: History
context.details: Year 11 class, Ms Clarke. Class taught in English.

transcript:
[Část 1]
Okay, okay, settle down please, settle down. Yes, Tomas, you can finish your sandwich, but quietly. Right. So, uh, today we are finally getting to the First World War, the causes of it, and I want to, I want to get through quite a lot, so tak, let's start.

Before we begin, one thing about the cafeteria, because I know half of you are thinking about it already. Yes, I heard the, the new schnitzel is apparently a crime against humanity. Somebody told me it was more breadcrumbs than schnitzel. Is that true? Yes? Okay. Well, that is not on today's agenda, but write a letter to the headmaster, I will sign it. Anyway. Back to the war.

So. The causes of the First World War. Historians have argued about this for more than a hundred years, and they still don't agree, which is, you know, good news for us because it means we get to have opinions. But there is a classic way to remember the main causes, and it's an acronym. M, A, I, N. Main. Very creative. M is for militarism, A is for alliances, I is for imperialism, and N is for nationalism. Write that down. M-A-I-N.

Okay, militarism first. By nineteen hundred, the great powers of Europe were building up their armies and their navies like crazy. Germany especially. Germany had a huge army, the best trained in Europe, and then the Kaiser, Wilhelm the Second, decided he wanted a big navy as well. And that was a problem for Britain, because Britain, uh, Britain had always said, we rule the waves, the Royal Navy must be bigger than any two other navies together. So you get this naval arms race. Dreadnoughts, the big battleship, HMS Dreadnought, nineteen oh six. Yes, Anna? No, a dreadnought is not a person, it's a ship. The name means, more or less, fear nothing. Okay.

And the point about militarism is not only the number of soldiers. It's also that the generals gained a lot of influence. They had plans, detailed plans, railway timetables, and once you start the timetable, it's very hard to stop it. Remember that, because we will come back to it with the Schlifen plan in a minute.

Second, alliances. This is the one that you really need to understand, so listen. Europe was divided into two armed camps. On one side you have the Triple Alliance, that's Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy. Formed in eighteen eighty-two. And on the other side you have the Triple Entente, the on-tont, French word, it means understanding, so not exactly a formal alliance, more like friendship with, with some promises. That's France, Russia and Britain. France and Russia first, in the nineteen-nineties, I mean the eighteen-nineties, sorry, eighteen ninety-four, then Britain and France in nineteen oh four, the Entente Cordiale, and then Britain and Russia in nineteen oh seven.

Yes, Petra, you have a question. Italy? Good question, yes, Italy was in the Triple Alliance but in the end it did not fight with Germany and Austria. In nineteen fifteen Italy actually switched sides and joined the Entente. So, you know, a bit of a disloyal friend. Typical Italy, no, I'm joking, I'm joking, don't write that down.

The idea of alliances was supposed to keep peace, right, because nobody would dare attack if everyone is protected. But the result was that a small quarrel between two countries could drag in everyone else. It's like, hmm, it's like a fight in the cafeteria queue. One person pushes another, and suddenly the whole class is in it, because everybody has a friend. Okay, that's maybe a bit too, too close to real life.

Third, imperialism. The European powers were competing for colonies in Africa and Asia. Britain and France had huge empires. Germany came late, only united in eighteen seventy-one, and wanted its, what the Germans called a place in the sun. So you have the Moroccan crises, nineteen oh five and nineteen eleven, where Germany and France nearly went to war over Morocco. These crises made the relations worse and they pushed Britain and France closer together. Also in the Balkans, Austria-Hungary and Russia both wanted influence, because the Ottoman Empire was getting weaker, the sick man of Europe they called it.

And fourth, nationalism. This is a big one, and for our story it's probably the most explosive one. In the Balkans, many Slavic peoples wanted their own state, and Serbia was a small, independent state that wanted to unite all the South Slavs. Serbs, Croats, Bosnians, everybody. The problem was that millions of those people lived inside Austria-Hungary. So Austria-Hungary saw Serbia as a real threat to its existence. And in nineteen oh eight Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia, which made the Serbs furious. And Russia saw itself as the protector of the Slavs, so, you see, now the alliances kick in. Serbia, backed by Siberia, sorry, backed by Russia, I almost sent them to, to Siberia, that would be a geography lesson. Okay. Russia backs Serbia, Germany backs Austria.

Right, so that's the background, the, let's say, the gunpowder. Now we need the spark. And the spark is Sarajevo.

On the twenty-eighth of June, nineteen fourteen, Archduke Franz Ferdinand visited Sarajevo, the capital of Bosnia. And who was he? Well, he was the Kaiser's nephew. Franz Ferdinand was the Kaiser's nephew. Hmm, wait. No, no, that's wrong, that's wrong, I mixed it up. The Kaiser, Wilhelm, is the German one. Franz Ferdinand was Austrian. He was the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his uncle was the Emperor Franz Joseph. Sorry. Good that you are awake. Somebody write it correctly: heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, nephew of Franz Joseph, not the German Kaiser.

So he comes with his wife Sophie, in an open car. And there is a group of young conspirators waiting along the route, members of, of Young Bosnia, connected to a Serbian secret society called the Black Hand. First, one of them throws a bomb, and it misses, it bounces off, explodes under another car. The archduke goes on to the town hall, gives a, a rather angry speech, and then they decide to change the route to visit the injured people in hospital. But the driver was not told about the change, he takes a wrong turn, he stops and tries to reverse, right in front of a café, and who is standing outside the café eating a sandwich? Hm, yes, Tomas, a sandwich, don't, don't make that face. A nineteen-year-old Bosnian Serb called Gabriel Principe. Gavrilo Princip, that is the real name, but write it as you hear it, whatever. He steps forward and shoots the archduke and Sophie. Both die within minutes.

And I want you to remember this: the date of the assassination, twenty-eighth June nineteen fourteen, will definitely be in the exam. Definitely. I'm not joking. If you don't know it, I will be very sad and you will be very sad. Twenty-eighth of June, nineteen fourteen. Say it with me. Okay, not everyone. Fine.

So what happens next? This is what we call the July Crisis, and it's a chain reaction, almost like dominoes. First, Austria-Hungary wants to punish Serbia, but it is afraid of Russia. So what does it do? It asks Germany. And on the fifth and sixth of July, Germany gives Austria-Hungary what we call the blank cheque. You know what a cheque is? A check, in American. A piece of paper where you write an amount and the bank pays. A blank cheque means, you fill in the amount, we will pay. So Germany says, do whatever you want against Serbia, we will support you, whatever happens. Very, very dangerous promise. The Germans hoped it would be a short local war.

Then on the twenty-third of July, Austria sends Serbia an ultimatum, with ten demands, and they were deliberately made so harsh that Serbia couldn't accept all of them. Serbia accepted most, almost everything, but not all. And on the twenty-eighth of July, exactly one month after the murders, Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia. Now Russia starts to mobilise its army to protect Serbia. And Germany says, if you mobilise, we have to react. On the first of August, Germany declares war on Russia. Then on the third of August, on France.

And now the Schlifen Plan. Schlieffen, S-C-H-L-I-E-F-F-E-N, and yes, Marek, I will put it on the board, it's hard to spell, it's named after Count Alfred von Schlieffen, the chief of the German general staff some years earlier. The German problem was a war on two fronts. France in the west, Russia in the east. The plan was, defeat France fast, in about six weeks, before Russia is ready, because Russia is big and slow to mobilise. And then take all the trains and send the army east. But to defeat France quickly, the Germans wanted to go around the French fortifications through neutral Belgium. And that's the point. Belgium was neutral, guaranteed by the Treaty of London of eighteen thirty-nine, which Britain had signed. A, you know, scrap of paper, that's what the German chancellor called it.

So the Germans invaded Belgium on the fourth of August nineteen fourteen. And Britain had until then been hesitating. The British government was not sure, some ministers did not want war at all. But the invasion of Belgium changed everything. Britain sent an ultimatum to Germany, no answer came, and at eleven p.m. London time, on the fourth of August, Britain was at war with Germany. That's the date, fourth of August, remember it as well, though it's, it's not as, as sacred as the twenty-eighth of June.

Okay, so, to sum it up. Long-term causes, the MAIN things, militarism, alliances, imperialism, nationalism. The short-term trigger, the assassination in Sarajevo. And then the July Crisis, where everyone, to some degree, made it worse. Germany with the blank cheque, Austria with the ultimatum, Russia with the mobilisation. And there is no single villain, or maybe there is, depends which historian you ask. Which brings me to the homework.

Are you writing? Good. Homework. An essay, eight hundred words, eight-zero-zero, title, Which cause was the most important? Which of the four, militarism, alliances, imperialism or nationalism, was the most important cause of the First World War? You must argue, not just describe. Give evidence, give dates. Deadline is Monday the third of November. Yes, Eva, Monday, third of November. No, I will not accept it by email at midnight on Monday with the excuse that the internet was down. I have heard it all.

And, one more thing, next Tuesday we will have a short quiz on the alliance system. Who was in the Triple Alliance, who was in the Triple Entente, and when it was formed, roughly. Not very long, fifteen minutes. So go home, learn the two blocks, maybe draw a map, it helps.

Questions? Yes, Jakub? Whether the war was inevitable? That is a very good question, and honestly it's exactly the kind of thing you could use in your essay. Some historians say yes, the system was so tense that something would sooner or later happen. Others say no, if the driver had not taken a wrong turn, if the bomb had hit, if a few politicians had been cleverer, then maybe not. I like the, the idea that it was not inevitable, but, but I'm a romantic. Okay.

Right, we have about, what, five minutes left. Tak pojďme dál, let's look at the map on page forty-two, and after that you can go for lunch, and Tomas, please, please, don't buy the schnitzel.
traps: Homework: 800-word essay 'Which cause was the most important?' due Monday 3 November (note: in 2026 3 Nov is actually a Tuesday; teacher says Monday)
Quiz on the alliance system next Tuesday, about 15 minutes
Teacher says 'the date of the assassination will definitely be in the exam' - 28 June 1914
Teacher misspeaks 'Franz Ferdinand was the Kaiser's nephew' then corrects: heir to Austro-Hungarian throne, nephew of Emperor Franz Joseph
ASR: Serbia written as 'Siberia' once (teacher then jokes about sending them to Siberia, so the joke is real speech)
ASR: 'Gabriel Principe' instead of Gavrilo Princip
ASR: 'Schlifen' instead of Schlieffen (spelled correctly later by teacher)
Teacher slips 'nineteen-nineties' then corrects to eighteen-nineties; Franco-Russian alliance 1894
Acronym MAIN: militarism, alliances, imperialism, nationalism
Triple Alliance: Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy (1882); Italy switched to the Entente in 1915
Triple Entente: France, Russia, Britain; Entente Cordiale 1904, Anglo-Russian 1907
Blank cheque given by Germany on 5-6 July; ultimatum to Serbia 23 July; Austria declared war on Serbia 28 July
Germany declared war on Russia 1 August and France 3 August; Britain at war on 4 August 1914 after invasion of Belgium (Treaty of London 1839)
Schlieffen Plan: beat France in about six weeks, then turn to Russia
Cafeteria chatter: new schnitzel is mostly breadcrumbs; joke about letter to headmaster; Tomas eating a sandwich
Teacher jokes that the Italy remark should not be written down
Reference to map on page forty-two at the end
